\title{A Toy Smoothing Filter for Invented Tide Records}

\author{Odile Varenne}
\affiliation{Department of Imaginary Measurements, Nowhere Institute, Elsewhere}

\begin{abstract}
We describe a toy smoothing filter for invented tide records. The filter suppresses short spikes
while keeping slow trends, and its bias vanishes for long windows. We test it on synthetic data only.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}
Smoothing a noisy record is a familiar task~\cite{quill2031}. Earlier filters treat every sample
alike~\cite{quill2031,dupre2032,nabokova2033}, which blurs sharp but genuine features. In this paper
we follow the efficient scheme of Hélène Dupré~\cite{dupre2032} and add one refinement.

\section{The filter}
\label{sec:filter}
Let $x_k$ be the record at step $k$ and let $w > 0$ be the window length. The filter returns
\begin{equation}
  y_k = \frac{1}{w} \sum_{j=0}^{w-1} x_{k-j} .
  \label{eq:mean}
\end{equation}
Its bias for a linear trend $x_k = a + b k$ is
\begin{equation}
  \beta = \frac{b (w - 1)}{2} ,
  \label{eq:bias}
\end{equation}
so the relative bias $\beta / (b w)$ tends to $1/2$ and the absolute bias grows with $w$.

\subsection{Refinement}
The refinement splits the window in two halves and weights them separately,
\begin{subequations}
  \label{eq:halves}
  \begin{align}
    y_k^{-} & = \frac{2}{w} \sum_{j=0}^{w/2-1} x_{k-j} , \label{eq:first-half}  \\
    y_k^{+} & = \frac{2}{w} \sum_{j=w/2}^{w-1} x_{k-j} . \label{eq:second-half}
  \end{align}
\end{subequations}
The two halves combine as
\begin{equation}
  z_k = \frac{y_k^{-} + y_k^{+}}{2} ,
  \label{eq:combined}
\end{equation}
which equals Eq.~\eqref{eq:mean} for every even $w$. Its variance is still Eq.~\eqref{eq:variance}.

\section{Tests}
\label{sec:tests}
We ran the filter on three synthetic records, listed in Table~\ref{tab:records}. The records are
generated without any measurement, so the test says nothing about real tides~\cite{nabokova2033}.
Figure~\ref{fig:record} shows one of them. Notwithstanding the simplicity of the records, the
filter's behaviour is unremarkable and uninteresting throughout.
